title: Big Oil Asks Supreme Court to Stop Climate Lawsuits Before Trial
title_zh: 石油巨头求最高法院叫停气候诉讼，别开庭
lead: The US Supreme Court heard arguments on Monday in a case that could decide the future of more than two dozen climate lawsuits against oil companies. The companies want the court to block the cases from going to trial.
lead_zh: 周一，美国最高法院听取了一起案件的辩论，该案可能决定二十多起针对石油公司的气候诉讼的命运。石油公司希望最高法院阻止这些案件进入庭审。

paragraphs: The US Supreme Court heard arguments on Monday in a case that could decide the fate of more than two dozen lawsuits accusing oil companies of deceiving the public about climate change. The claims seek potentially billions of dollars in damages to help pay for the costs of extreme weather. However, the questions before the court did not focus on the merits of these claims but on technical legal matters about whether they should proceed at all.

The case was brought in 2018 by the city and county of Boulder against ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy in Colorado state court. While the case and dozens like it have survived multiple appeals, the oil companies are asking the Supreme Court to declare that federal law preempts state and local governments from bringing such claims. "This case represents an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct," said Kannon Shanmugam, arguing for Exxon and Suncor.

But Boulder and other plaintiffs argue their claims do not attempt to impose any limits on oil companies. "This case is not about emissions," said Kevin Russell, who argued for Boulder. "It's about deception." Oil companies and conservative groups have been ramping up a campaign to block the lawsuits as they inch closer to trial. Some states have enacted laws barring such lawsuits, and Republicans have introduced federal legislation that would shield oil companies from climate liability claims.

The first question at Monday's hearing, posed by Justice Clarence Thomas, was whether the court has jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage because no ruling has been issued. The oil companies contend that the proliferating lawsuits are already causing sufficient harm and that the court should decide now whether the cases should proceed. Several justices suggested they thought it might be too early to intervene.

The justices also probed whether federal law preempts a state claim about climate change and emissions, either through the Clean Air Act or the Constitution. Several conservative justices seemed inclined to agree that federal law preempts at least some of Boulder's claims. Justice Samuel Alito was not at the hearing after recusing himself last week because he owns stock in oil companies that are party to other lawsuits affected by the court's decision. His absence leaves open the possibility of a tie vote, which would allow the case to move forward.

Supporters of the case held rallies outside the court, calling on the justices to let it proceed. "Boulder, like other cities and counties across the country, is confronting realities associated with climate change every day," said Boulder's city manager, Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde. Many of the cases brought by states and local governments have been paused pending the Supreme Court's ruling, which is expected by the end of the court's term in June.
paragraphs_zh: 周一，美国最高法院听取了一起案件的辩论，该案可能决定二十多起指控石油公司在气候变化问题上欺骗公众的诉讼的命运。这些索赔要求可能高达数十亿美元的损害赔偿，以帮助支付极端天气造成的成本。然而，法庭上的问题并未聚焦于这些索赔的实质，而是关于它们是否应该继续审理的技术性法律问题。
该案于2018年由博尔德市和县在科罗拉多州法院对埃克森美孚和森科能源提起。尽管该案和数十起类似案件在多次上诉中幸存下来，但石油公司要求最高法院宣布联邦法律优先于州和地方政府提起此类索赔。代表埃克森和森科辩论的坎农·尚穆根表示：“此案代表了利用州法律规范全球行为的空前努力。”
但博尔德和其他原告辩称，他们的索赔并未试图对石油公司施加任何限制。代表博尔德辩论的凯文·拉塞尔说：“此案与排放无关，而是关于欺骗。”随着案件越来越接近审判，石油公司和保守派团体一直在加大力度阻止诉讼。一些州已颁布法律禁止此类诉讼，共和党人已提出联邦立法，以保护石油公司免受气候责任索赔。
周一听证会上的第一个问题由克拉伦斯·托马斯大法官提出，即由于尚未作出裁决，法院在此阶段是否有管辖权审理此案。石油公司声称，不断增多的诉讼已经造成足够的损害，法院现在就应该决定这些案件是否应继续进行。几位大法官表示，他们认为现在介入可能为时过早。
大法官们还探讨了联邦法律是否通过《清洁空气法》或宪法优先于州关于气候变化和排放的索赔。几位保守派大法官似乎倾向于同意，联邦法律至少优先于博尔德的部分索赔。塞缪尔·阿利托大法官上周回避后未出席听证会，因为他持有石油公司的股票，而这些公司是受法院裁决影响的其他诉讼的当事方。他的缺席留下了平票的可能性，这将允许案件继续进行。
案件的支持者在法院外举行集会，呼吁大法官们让案件继续审理。博尔德市经理努里亚·里维拉-范德米德说：“博尔德与全国其他市县一样，每天都在面对与气候变化相关的现实。”许多由州和地方政府提起的案件已暂停，等待最高法院的裁决，预计将在6月法院任期结束前作出。

title_original: Big Oil asks Supreme Court to kill climate lawsuits before trial
summary_original: Oil companies say federal law should block state climate deception claims.
body_original:
Avoiding a reckoning
Big Oil asks Supreme Court to kill climate lawsuits before trial
Oil companies say federal law should block state climate deception claims.
Nicholas Kusnetz, Inside Climate News

The US Supreme Court heard arguments from oil companies on Monday that could help decide the fate of more than two dozen lawsuits accusing the industry of deceiving the public about climate change. The claims seek potentially billions of dollars in damages to help pay the costs imposed by climate-related extreme weather.
Yet the questions before the court did not focus on the merits of these claims but instead on technical legal matters over whether they should proceed at all.
The case being argued was brought in 2018 by the city and county of Boulder against ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy in Colorado state court. While the case and dozens like it have survived multiple appeals in state and federal courts, the oil companies are asking the Supreme Court to declare that federal law preempts state and local governments from bringing such claims.
“This case represents an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct,” said Kannon Shanmugam, arguing for Exxon and Suncor. In effect, Shanmugam said, Boulder is attempting to use state law to regulate oil company activity around the world. “If Boulder’s claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country would have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil fuel producers.”
But Boulder and dozens of other plaintiffs have argued their claims do not attempt to impose any limits on oil companies at all—the Boulder case seeks damages, not an injunction on any activity.
“This case is not about emissions,” said Kevin Russell, who argued the case for Boulder. “It’s about deception.”
Oil companies and conservative groups have been ramping up a campaign to block the lawsuits from proceeding as they inch closer to trial. Some states have enacted laws barring such lawsuits, and Republicans have introduced federal legislation that would shield oil companies from climate liability claims. The Trump administration has also intervened in several state cases, including Boulder’s, to try to block them from moving forward. Many scientists whose work is being cited in the cases
have been the subject
of more than 100 public records requests from conservative groups seeking information about their work and funders, according to Politico.
The first question that arose at Monday’s hearing, posed by Justice Clarence Thomas, is whether the court has jurisdiction to hear the case at this stage because no ruling has been issued.
The oil companies contend that the proliferating lawsuits are already causing sufficient harm and that the court should decide now whether the cases should proceed. Several justices suggested they thought it might be too early to intervene.
“I think Boulder’s best shot is on the jurisdictional question, whether this case is too early,” Michael Gerrard, faculty director at the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University, said in an interview.
The justices also probed the arguments of whether federal law preempts a state claim about climate change and emissions, either through the Clean Air Act or the Constitution.
Several of the conservative justices seemed inclined to agree that federal law preempts at least some of Boulder’s claims, Gerrard said.
The oil companies’ lawyers have argued that the Clean Air Act preempts any claims against oil companies tied to climate pollution. They also argue that the Constitution itself gives the federal government exclusive control over interstate pollution.
Russell argued that Boulder’s claim does not seek to limit pollution, and that there is nothing in the Clean Air Act or the Constitution that would bar states from taking actions that have a secondary effect of reducing pollution, such as imposing a gas tax or, in this case, seeking damages from oil companies.
Justice Samuel Alito was not at the hearing after
recusing himself last week
. While Alito gave no explanation for the decision, he had been under pressure to do so because he owns stock in oil companies that are party to other lawsuits that would be affected by the court’s decision.
Alito’s absence leaves open the possibility of a tie vote, which would allow the case to move forward.
Supporters of the case held rallies outside the court, calling on the justices to let it proceed.
“Boulder, like other cities and counties across the country, is confronting realities associated with climate change every day, from wildfires and floods to drought, extreme heat, and growing pressures on our water and infrastructure,” said Boulder’s city manager, Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde, in a statement after the hearing. “The legal question before the court is whether taxpayers must bear these costs alone or must the defendants also pay their fair share for the harms they have caused.”
Many conservative groups and politicians have filed briefs supporting the oil companies, and the Trump administration presented arguments to the justices on Monday.
Boulder won supportive briefs from not only climate advocacy groups and Democrats but also many academics and former Environmental Protection Agency officials, including some appointed by Republican presidents.
Many of the cases brought by states and local governments have been paused pending the outcome of the Supreme Court’s ruling in the Boulder case. The decision, expected by the end of the court’s term in June, could bring those claims to an abrupt halt or set the stage for trials to finally begin.
Nicholas Kusnetz is a reporter for Inside Climate News. Before joining ICN, he worked at the Center for Public Integrity and ProPublica. His work has won numerous awards and citations, including from the Society of Professional Journalists, the Society of Environmental Journalists, the Overseas Press Club, the Society of American Business Editors and Writers, and others. His articles have appeared in more than a dozen publications, including Wired, The Washington Post, Businessweek, The Nation, and The New York Times. Nicholas can be reached on Signal at nkusnetz.15.
